foods.name: Whole Wheat Bread
foods.notes: Major fructan source. Sourdough fermentation reduces FODMAPs and lectins.

foods.name: White Rice
foods.notes: Well tolerated staple. Low nickel content.

foods.name: Brown Rice
foods.notes: Higher nickel than white rice. Soaking reduces lectins.

foods.name: Oats
foods.notes: Very high nickel. Multiple FODMAP sources. Certified gluten-free varieties available.

foods.name: Barley
foods.notes: High fructans and GOS. Contraindicated in FODMAP and gluten-sensitive diets.

foods.name: Rye
foods.notes: Highest FODMAP fructans among grains. Sourdough fermentation greatly reduces FODMAPs.

foods.name: Corn (Grain)
foods.notes: Less FODMAP-problematic than wheat. Common allergen in some populations.

foods.name: Quinoa
foods.notes: Naturally gluten-free. Saponins can cause digestive issues; rinse before cooking.

foods.name: Buckwheat
foods.notes: Gluten-free. Low FODMAP. Moderate oxalates.

foods.name: Millet
foods.notes: Gluten-free, low FODMAP option.

foods.name: Teff
foods.notes: Gluten-free, nutritious. High oxalates.

foods.name: Amaranth
foods.notes: Gluten-free. Contains oxalates and lectins.

foods.name: Spelt
foods.notes: Contains gluten. Often tolerated better than wheat when fermented.

foods.name: Kamut
foods.notes: Ancient wheat variety. Still contains gluten and high FODMAPs.

foods.name: Polenta
foods.notes: Corn derivative. Gluten-free option.

foods.name: Milk (Cow)
foods.notes: Primary allergen. High lactose content. Fresh milk lowest histamine.

foods.name: Butter
foods.notes: Fat-based, minimal lactose. Ghee has minimal dairy proteins.

foods.name: Yogurt (Plain)
foods.notes: Fermented increases histamine and amines. Greek yogurt lower lactose.

foods.name: Cheese (Cheddar)
foods.notes: Aged cheese = VERY HIGH histamine and amines. Minimal lactose.

foods.name: Cheese (Fresh Mozzarella)
foods.notes: Fresh cheese much lower histamine than aged varieties.

foods.name: Cream Cheese
foods.notes: Soft cheese. Moderate histamine and amines.

foods.name: Milk (Goat)
foods.notes: Often tolerated better than cow milk by those with cow allergy. Contains lactose.

foods.name: Cottage Cheese
foods.notes: Lower lactose than milk. Moderate histamine and amines.

foods.name: Greek Yogurt
foods.notes: Fermentation produces higher histamine and amines. Much lower lactose.

foods.name: Ricotta Cheese
foods.notes: Whey-based cheese. Moderate lactose.

foods.name: Feta Cheese
foods.notes: Aged cheese, high histamine and amines. Low lactose.

foods.name: Whey Protein Powder
foods.notes: Processed form. Isolate has minimal lactose and dairy proteins.

foods.name: Chicken Breast (Fresh)
foods.notes: Low allergen profile. Fresh is best for histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Beef (Lean)
foods.notes: Well tolerated fresh meat. Low histamine content.

foods.name: Pork (Fresh)
foods.notes: Fresh pork well-tolerated. Avoid processed/cured versions (high histamine).

foods.name: Turkey (Fresh)
foods.notes: Excellent low-allergen protein option.

foods.name: Lamb (Fresh)
foods.notes: Low-allergen red meat option.

foods.name: Ham (Cured)
foods.notes: High histamine and amines from curing. Contains sulfites. Avoid if histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Bacon
foods.notes: Cured and smoked = VERY HIGH histamine and amines. Avoid if histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Sausage (Fresh)
foods.notes: Fresh sausage has additives. Often contains gluten binders.

foods.name: Ground Beef
foods.notes: Lower histamine than ground pork. Use fresh.

foods.name: Duck (Fresh)
foods.notes: Well-tolerated poultry. Slightly higher in fat.

foods.name: Liver (Beef)
foods.notes: Nutrient-dense but moderate histamine and amines.

foods.name: Prosciutto
foods.notes: Aged cured meat = VERY HIGH histamine and amines. Avoid if histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Salmon (Fresh)
foods.notes: Fish allergen present. Fresh lowest histamine.

foods.name: Tuna (Canned)
foods.notes: VERY HIGH histamine and amines. High nickel from can. Avoid if histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Cod (Fresh)
foods.notes: White fish. Low histamine when fresh.

foods.name: Mackerel
foods.notes: VERY HIGH histamine and amines. Oily fish. Avoid if histamine-sensitive.

foods.name: Salmon (Smoked)
foods.notes: Smoking increases histamine. Contains sulfites.

foods.name: Shrimp (Fresh)
foods.notes: Major shellfish allergen. Moderate nickel. Low histamine when fresh.

foods.name: Crab
foods.notes: Major shellfish allergen. Moderate nickel and histamine.

foods.name: Oysters
foods.notes: Shellfish allergen. HIGH nickel. Moderate oxalates and histamine.

foods.name: Mussels
foods.notes: Shellfish allergen. VERY HIGH nickel. High histamine and amines.

foods.name: Lobster
foods.notes: Major shellfish allergen. Moderate histamine.

foods.name: Anchovies
foods.notes: Cured/fermented = VERY HIGH histamine and amines. High nickel.

foods.name: Trout (Fresh)
foods.notes: Fresh fish. Low histamine when not aged or processed.

foods.name: Banana
foods.notes: Ripe bananas higher in amines. Latex cross-reactivity.

foods.name: Strawberry
foods.notes: High histamine and salicylates. Problematic for FODMAP-sensitive individuals.

foods.name: Orange
foods.notes: Histamine liberator. High salicylates. Cross-reactivity potential.

foods.name: Lemon
foods.notes: High salicylates. Histamine liberator effects.

foods.name: Tomato
foods.notes: Higher histamine in canned/processed. Nightshade alkaloids.

foods.name: Apple
foods.notes: High fructose and polyols (sorbitol). Birch pollen cross-reactivity.

foods.name: Pear
foods.notes: Very high fructose and sorbitol content.

foods.name: Mango
foods.notes: Very high fructose. Potential latex cross-reactivity.

foods.name: Watermelon
foods.notes: High fructose and mannitol content.

foods.name: Raisins
foods.notes: Very high sulfites in dried form. Concentrated histamine and amines.

foods.name: Blueberry
foods.notes: High salicylates. Antioxidant-rich.

foods.name: Grapes
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates and sulfites, especially wine grapes.

foods.name: Pineapple
foods.notes: High histamine. Bromelain enzyme can cause oral irritation.

foods.name: Kiwi
foods.notes: Moderate oxalates and salicylates. Actinidin enzyme allergen.

foods.name: Peach
foods.notes: Moderate sorbitol content.

foods.name: Cherry
foods.notes: High polyols and salicylates.

foods.name: Spinach
foods.notes: EXTREMELY high oxalates. Kidney stone risk. Higher histamine when cooked/stored.

foods.name: Garlic
foods.notes: EXTREMELY high fructans. Even small amounts problematic for IBS.

foods.name: Onion
foods.notes: EXTREMELY high fructans. Moderate reduction when cooked.

foods.name: Potato
foods.notes: Nightshade with moderate lectins. Solanine in green/sprouted varieties.

foods.name: Bell Pepper
foods.notes: Nightshade with high salicylates. Raw higher in lectins than cooked.

foods.name: Mushroom
foods.notes: High mannitol. Histamine increases with age/cooking.

foods.name: Asparagus
foods.notes: Moderate fructans and oxalates. Purines present.

foods.name: Beets
foods.notes: High oxalates and natural nitrates. Can accumulate pesticides.

foods.name: Sweet Potato
foods.notes: Low FODMAP in small portions. Generally well-tolerated.

foods.name: Cauliflower
foods.notes: Moderate mannitol and GOS. Well-cooked reduces bloating.

foods.name: Broccoli
foods.notes: Moderate fructans and GOS. Goitrogenic compounds.

foods.name: Celery
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates and polyols. Apiaceae family allergen.

foods.name: Carrot
foods.notes: Low FODMAP. Well-tolerated. Apiaceae family potential cross-reactivity.

foods.name: Zucchini
foods.notes: Low allergen profile. Well-tolerated by most.

foods.name: Lettuce
foods.notes: Very low allergen profile. Excellent for restricted diets.

foods.name: Cabbage
foods.notes: Moderate fructans. Histamine increases when fermented (sauerkraut).

foods.name: Corn (Vegetable)
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates. May contain glyphosate if not organic.

foods.name: Lentils
foods.notes: Very high GOS. Soaking/pressure cooking reduces lectins significantly.

foods.name: Chickpeas
foods.notes: High fructans and GOS. Pressure cooking recommended.

foods.name: Black Beans
foods.notes: High nickel and GOS content. Soaking reduces antinutrients.

foods.name: Kidney Beans
foods.notes: VERY HIGH lectins when raw. Must be cooked thoroughly. Pressure cooking essential.

foods.name: Soybeans
foods.notes: High nickel and histamine. Fermented soy products increase histamine further.

foods.name: Green Peas
foods.notes: Lower lectin content than dried legumes. Moderate fructans and GOS.

foods.name: Pinto Beans
foods.notes: Similar profile to black beans. High GOS content.

foods.name: Peanuts
foods.notes: Common allergen. Moderate oxalates and salicylates.

foods.name: Split Peas
foods.notes: Pre-split, lower lectin content. Moderate FODMAP triggers.

foods.name: Mung Beans
foods.notes: Easier to digest than other legumes. Sprouting dramatically reduces lectins.

foods.name: Cashews
foods.notes: VERY HIGH nickel content. One of the highest nickel sources in nuts.

foods.name: Almonds
foods.notes: HIGH oxalates and nickel. Blanching reduces oxalates.

foods.name: Sunflower Seeds
foods.notes: High nickel content. Moderate oxalates and salicylates.

foods.name: Flaxseeds
foods.notes: Moderate nickel and oxalates. Well tolerated by most.

foods.name: Pumpkin Seeds
foods.notes: Moderate nickel and oxalates. Good nutrient profile.

foods.name: Coconut
foods.notes: HIGH salicylates. Moderate cross-reactivity with tree nuts.

foods.name: Pine Nuts
foods.notes: Moderate nickel. Can cause metallic taste syndrome if stored improperly.

foods.name: Sesame Seeds
foods.notes: Moderate oxalates and nickel. Salicylate level moderate to high.

foods.name: Macadamia Nuts
foods.notes: Lower oxalates and salicylates compared to other nuts.

foods.name: Soy Sauce
foods.notes: HIGH histamine from fermentation and amines. Contains gluten unless tamari.

foods.name: Vinegar
foods.notes: HIGH histamine. White distilled vinegar lowest in histamine.

foods.name: Fish Sauce
foods.notes: VERY HIGH histamine. Fermented fish product with extreme amine levels.

foods.name: Mustard
foods.notes: HIGH salicylates. Moderate nickel from mustard seeds.

foods.name: Worcestershire Sauce
foods.notes: HIGH histamine and amines from fermentation and anchovies.

foods.name: Hot Sauce
foods.notes: HIGH salicylates and histamine from chilis and fermentation.

foods.name: Miso
foods.notes: HIGH histamine and nickel from soy and fermentation.

foods.name: Tahini
foods.notes: Moderate oxalates and nickel. Generally well tolerated.

foods.name: Mayonnaise
foods.notes: Contains eggs. Moderate histamine from oxidation and age.

foods.name: Red Wine (Aged/Premium)
foods.notes: HIGH histamine and sulfites. Avoid if histamine intolerant.

foods.name: Beer
foods.notes: HIGH gluten and histamine. Contains sulfites and amines.

foods.name: Coffee
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates and oxalates. Contains caffeine.

foods.name: Black Tea (Loose Leaf)
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates and oxalates. Lower oxidation than some teas.

foods.name: Green Tea (Loose Leaf)
foods.notes: Moderate oxalates. Less oxidized than black tea.

foods.name: Kombucha (Fermented)
foods.notes: VERY HIGH histamine from fermentation. Avoid if histamine intolerant.

foods.name: Orange Juice
foods.notes: Moderate fructose and salicylates. High sugar content.

foods.name: Cow Milk
foods.notes: VERY HIGH lactose. Contains histamine depending on fermentation.

foods.name: Cinnamon (Cassia/Heavy)
foods.notes: VERY HIGH salicylates. One of the highest spice sources.

foods.name: Turmeric (Root/Concentrated)
foods.notes: HIGH oxalates and salicylates. Moderate nickel.

foods.name: Black Pepper (Whole/Ground)
foods.notes: HIGH salicylates. Moderate nickel content.

foods.name: Ginger
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates and fructans. Generally well tolerated.

foods.name: Corn Tortilla
foods.notes: Corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free when prepared traditionally via nixtamalization. Moderate nickel content from corn grain. FODMAP fructans present but generally well-tolerated in modest portions. Risk of cross-contamination with wheat flour in commercial settings. Nixtamalization process reduces lectins and improves mineral bioavailability.

foods.name: Flour Tortilla
foods.notes: High gluten content (wheat flour base). Typically contains lard or shortening adding moderate dairy/fat content and potential trace soy from commercial shortenings. High FODMAP fructans from wheat flour. Not suitable for celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. Lactose content varies depending on fat source used in preparation.

foods.name: Refried Beans (Frijoles Refritos)
foods.notes: Very high GOS (galacto-oligosaccharides) content - major FODMAP concern. High lectin levels if undercooked; proper extended cooking or pressure cooking significantly reduces this. High nickel content from legumes. Histamine increases with storage time and fermentation. Often prepared with lard, adding fat-soluble allergen concerns. Soaking and cooking techniques substantially reduce allergen load.

foods.name: Guacamole
foods.notes: Avocado is a histamine liberator - acts as a trigger even if not high in baseline histamine. Moderate amines and salicylates present. Fresh guacamole significantly better tolerated than stored. Critical latex-fruit cross-reactivity concern for latex-sensitive individuals. Browning/oxidation increases allergen load. Citrus additions increase salicylate content.

foods.name: Salsa Verde (Tomatillo)
foods.notes: Tomatillo-based green salsas lower in histamine than red tomato salsas. Moderate salicylates from both tomatillo and typical cilantro addition. Nightshade family consideration despite being green. Fresh preparation preferred over stored. Cooking increases histamine and salicylate content. Cilantro contributes significant salicylates.

foods.name: Pico de Gallo
foods.notes: Fresh tomato-based preparation with moderate histamine and amines. Salicylates elevated from tomato, onion, cilantro, and lime. Nightshade family cross-reactivity. Best consumed immediately after preparation; histamine and amine content increases significantly with storage. Cilantro and lime additions contribute substantial salicylate load. Standard salsa for fresh preparations.

foods.name: Mole Sauce
foods.notes: Complex sauce with multiple high-allergen components. Chocolate adds high nickel, histamine, oxalates. Dried chilis contribute high salicylates and nightshade reactivity. Often contains nuts (almonds, peanuts) - significant tree nut/peanut allergen. High amines from fermented chilis and chocolate. Extended cooking increases histamine. Multiple cross-reactivity concerns. Not suitable for nut-allergic, high-histamine sensitive, or nightshade-reactive individuals. Requires careful ingredient verification.

foods.name: Queso Fresco
foods.notes: Fresh cheese format retains higher lactose than aged varieties. High dairy allergen load. Moderate histamine and amines for a fresh cheese (much lower than aged varieties). Significant lactose content - problematic for lactose intolerance. If aged (uncommon for queso fresco), histamine and amines increase substantially. May contain rennet and bacterial cultures. Important distinction from harder aged cheeses which concentrate histamine.

foods.name: Chorizo (Mexican)
foods.notes: Very high histamine - fermented/cured pork product with high amines from fermentation. High salicylates from paprika and spice blend. Contains nitrates/nitrites as preservatives. Major trigger for histamine intolerance and amine sensitivity. Multiple capsicum-based seasonings add salicylate load. Fermentation process significantly concentrates histamine and amines. Not suitable for low-histamine or FODMAP-restricted diets despite containing no FODMAPs.

foods.name: Carnitas
foods.notes: Extended slow-cooking preparation increases histamine and amine formation. Fresh preparation better tolerated than stored. Moderate histamine and amine levels from prolonged cooking and meat breakdown. Storage time further increases histamine - consume fresh when possible. Low salicylate content from simple spice profile. Not suitable for high-histamine sensitivity. Proper cooking eliminates bacterial risks but increases biogenic amine formation.

foods.name: Tamales
foods.notes: Traditional corn masa-based tamales are gluten-free, but many commercial versions use wheat flour. High FODMAP fructans from grain base. Typically prepared with lard adding dairy/fat content. Steaming preparation minimally increases allergen levels. Fillings vary (meat, cheese, rajas) - allergen profile changes with filling. Fresh consumption better than reheated. Check masa source for wheat flour additions.

foods.name: Enchilada Sauce (Red)
foods.notes: High salicylates from dried chilis - major trigger for sensitive individuals. Moderate-high histamine and amines from fermented/dried peppers. Nightshade family reactivity. Cooking process further concentrates histamine. Often includes garlic adding additional salicylates and amines. Very problematic for both salicylate-sensitive and histamine-intolerant individuals. Fresh preparation better tolerated than commercial canned versions.

foods.name: Nopales (Cactus Pads)
foods.notes: Unique low-allergen food with minimal histamine, amines, gluten, and dairy concerns. Moderate oxalate content - concern for oxalate-sensitive individuals, especially kidney stone prone patients. Low salicylates. Moderate FODMAP polyols. Fresh preparation preferable to canned. Boiling reduces oxalate content. Contains glochids (spines) that must be carefully removed. Very well-tolerated by most with standard allergies, but specific concerns for oxalate and polyol-sensitive individuals.

foods.name: Elote (Mexican Street Corn)
foods.notes: Corn kernel base is naturally gluten-free with moderate nickel and FODMAP fructans. Major allergen load comes from toppings: mayo adds egg and potential soy from commercial preparations, cheese adds dairy and lactose, lime/chili powder adds minor salicylates. Moderate lactose from dairy coating. Low histamine and amines. Allergen profile varies significantly by preparation method (mayo vs. crema). Check for egg in mayonnaise and soy additives.

foods.name: Chilaquiles
foods.notes: High gluten and dairy allergen load - combination dish with multiple problematic components. Flour tortillas provide high gluten and FODMAP fructans. Salsa (typically red) contributes high salicylates and nightshade reactivity. High dairy from cheese and sour cream toppings with significant lactose. Moderate histamine and amines from both sauce fermentation and cheese. High FODMAP overall. Egg addition varies. Not suitable for celiac disease, lactose intolerance, high-histamine sensitivity, salicylate sensitivity, or nightshade reactivity. Significant cross-contamination risk with multiple high-allergen components.

foods.name: Fried Rice

preparation_modifiers.soy_sauce_type: Regular soy sauce contains both soy and wheat
preparation_modifiers.fermentation: Soy sauce fermentation increases histamine and amines

foods.notes: Soy sauce is the primary allergen concern, containing both soy and gluten (wheat). Fermented soy sauce increases histamine significantly. Histamine level varies with soy sauce quality and age.

foods.name: Wonton Soup

preparation_modifiers.wonton_wrapper_composition: Wheat flour and egg-based; often contains added soy sauce
preparation_modifiers.filling_variation: Pork filling is standard; shrimp/shellfish variants increase shellfish allergen

foods.notes: Wonton wrappers contain wheat (gluten) and egg. Fillings typically contain pork but may include shrimp or shellfish. Broth may contain soy sauce, adding soy and histamine. Histamine increases with broth simmering time.

foods.name: Sweet and Sour Sauce

preparation_modifiers.sugar_source: Table sugar or high-fructose corn syrup increases fructose content
preparation_modifiers.vinegar_type: Vinegar fermentation increases histamine; aged vinegars highest
preparation_modifiers.pineapple_content: Fresh pineapple increases salicylates; canned reduces slightly

foods.notes: High fructose content from sugar and fruit (pineapple). Vinegar is fermented and moderately high in histamine. Salicylates present in vinegar, tomato (if included), and pineapple. Histamine increases with fermentation duration.

foods.name: Hoisin Sauce

preparation_modifiers.fermentation_duration: Extended fermentation increases histamine and amines significantly

foods.notes: Hoisin is a fermented condiment with high histamine and amines. Contains soy and wheat (gluten). High fructose content from sugar. Salicylates present from fermentation byproducts. One of the highest histamine condiments in Asian cuisine.

foods.name: Dim Sum - Shrimp Dumpling (Har Gow)

preparation_modifiers.wrapper_composition: Tapioca starch and wheat starch blend; may contain trace amounts of wheat
preparation_modifiers.storage_duration: Frozen storage stabilizes histamine; fresh dumplings slightly lower histamine
preparation_modifiers.dipping_sauce: Soy sauce increases histamine and amines

foods.notes: High shellfish allergen from shrimp. Wrapper may contain wheat starch. Histamine elevated in shrimp, especially with storage time. Nickel content from stainless steel preparation surfaces. Often served with soy sauce dip adding additional histamine.

foods.name: Sushi Rice

preparation_modifiers.vinegar_type: Rice vinegar fermentation increases histamine; older vinegars higher
preparation_modifiers.salt_content: Standard salt addition, minimal allergen impact

foods.notes: Rice is naturally low-allergen. Histamine elevation from rice vinegar fermentation. Fructose from added sugar. Nickel from preparation with stainless steel utensils. Otherwise one of the safest options for sensitive individuals when prepared without fish/shellfish fillings.

foods.name: Edamame (steamed, salted)

preparation_modifiers.cooking_method: Steaming is standard; boiling reduces some FODMAPs slightly
preparation_modifiers.fresh_vs_frozen: Frozen edamame may have slightly reduced lectins

foods.notes: Very high soy allergen. High GOS (galacto-oligosaccharides) FODMAP content, problematic for IBS and FODMAP-sensitive individuals. Legume lectins present. Moderate nickel content from soil accumulation in legumes. Histamine moderate from immature soybean processing.

foods.name: Teriyaki Sauce

preparation_modifiers.soy_sauce_base: Contains both soy and wheat; primary allergen source
preparation_modifiers.fermentation_duration: Fermented soy sauce increases histamine and amines dramatically

foods.notes: Teriyaki combines fermented soy sauce (high gluten and soy) with high sugar and mirin (sweet rice wine). Very high histamine and amines from fermentation. High fructose from sugar. May contain sake (fermented) increasing histamine further. One of the highest-allergen Asian condiments.

foods.name: Miso Soup

preparation_modifiers.miso_fermentation: Fermentation duration (months to years) drastically increases histamine
preparation_modifiers.miso_type: Mugi miso (barley) contains gluten; hatcho miso (100% soy) is highest histamine
preparation_modifiers.dashi_broth: Fish stock (kombu/bonito) adds fish allergen and histamine

foods.notes: Miso is heavily fermented soybean paste, extremely high in histamine and amines. Most miso contains gluten (mugi miso with barley). Dashi broth typically contains fish products. High GOS FODMAP from soy and wakame seaweed. Nickel from seaweed and cooking vessel. One of the highest-histamine foods in cuisine.

foods.name: Tempura Batter

preparation_modifiers.flour_type: Wheat flour is standard; some recipes use rice flour
preparation_modifiers.egg_content: Eggs are binding agent in batter
preparation_modifiers.dipping_sauce: Tempura sauce contains soy sauce, increasing soy and histamine
preparation_modifiers.frying_oil: Reused oil increases trans fats and oxidation byproducts

foods.notes: High gluten from wheat flour. Moderate egg content as binder. Soy sauce in dipping sauce adds soy and histamine. Histamine moderate from frying oils (oxidation). Cross-contamination risk if used with shellfish fillings. Gluten-free alternative batters available.

foods.name: Kimchi (with shrimp paste)

preparation_modifiers.fermentation_duration: Extended fermentation (weeks to months) dramatically increases histamine and amines
preparation_modifiers.shrimp_paste_content: Contains fermented shrimp paste (salted shrimp), very high histamine and shellfish
preparation_modifiers.spice_level: Red chili pepper adds high salicylates

foods.notes: Extremely high histamine from fermentation (weeks minimum). Contains fermented shrimp/fish products (very high histamine). Very high amines from fermentation. High salicylates from red chili peppers. Moderate FODMAPs (fructans) from garlic. One of the highest-allergen foods; problematic for histamine sensitivity, shellfish allergy, and nightshade sensitivity.

foods.name: Gochujang (Korean Chili Paste)

preparation_modifiers.fermentation_duration: Typically fermented 6-12 months or more; increases histamine exponentially
preparation_modifiers.soy_sauce_content: Contains fermented soy (gluten and soy); soy sauce increases histamine
preparation_modifiers.chili_content: Red chili peppers very high in salicylates

foods.notes: Fermented condiment with extremely high histamine and amines. Contains soy and wheat (gluten). Very high salicylates from chili peppers. High sugar content increases fructose. Lectins from fermented soy. One of the top histamine-containing condiments. Avoid with histamine intolerance.

foods.name: Bulgogi Marinade

preparation_modifiers.soy_sauce_content: Contains soy sauce (soy and gluten); fermentation increases histamine
preparation_modifiers.pear_content: Asian pear adds fructose and slight salicylates
preparation_modifiers.garlic_content: Garlic adds fructans and slight amines

foods.notes: Marinade contains fermented soy sauce (gluten, soy, histamine). Pear sweetener increases fructose (FODMAP). Garlic adds fructans. Moderate histamine from soy sauce fermentation. If meat is aged before marinating, beef histamine content increases. Salicylates from spices and pear.

foods.name: Coconut Milk (Canned)

preparation_modifiers.can_composition: BPA-lined cans increase nickel leaching into product
preparation_modifiers.storage_duration: Canned product increases histamine through oxidation; aged > 1 year higher
preparation_modifiers.fresh_vs_canned: Fresh coconut milk has lower nickel and histamine but shorter shelf life

foods.notes: FDA classifies coconut as tree nut for labeling purposes; clinical cross-reactivity with tree nuts is low but must be labeled. Canned versions contain moderate nickel from can lining and stainless steel processing. Histamine increases with storage. Fresh coconut milk significantly lower in nickel and histamine. Clinical note: despite tree nut classification, actual IgE cross-reactivity with true tree nuts (almonds, walnuts) is rare.

foods.name: Pad Thai Sauce

preparation_modifiers.peanut_content: Critical allergen; major source of peanut exposure
preparation_modifiers.fish_sauce_component: Fermented fish sauce very high in histamine and amines
preparation_modifiers.tamarind_content: Tamarind adds salicylates and slight histamine

foods.notes: Extremely high peanut allergen - major concern for peanut allergy. Fish sauce is fermented and very high histamine and amines. High fructose from sugar and tamarind. Salicylates from tamarind and spices. High cross-contamination risk during preparation. Soy sauce adds additional soy and gluten. Histamine increases with sauce age.

foods.name: Green Curry Paste

preparation_modifiers.herb_content: Green chili, cilantro, basil very high in salicylates
preparation_modifiers.canned_vs_fresh: Canned paste increases nickel from can lining

foods.notes: Very high salicylates from green chilis and herbs (cilantro, basil). Fructans from garlic and shallots (FODMAP). Moderate histamine from fermented components. Nickel elevated in canned versions. Oxalates from herbs. Green chili peppers are higher in salicylates than red. Problematic for salicylate sensitivity.

foods.name: Tom Yum Soup Base

preparation_modifiers.fish_sauce_content: Critical component - fermented fish sauce extremely high histamine
preparation_modifiers.shrimp_paste_content: Often contains fermented shrimp paste, very high histamine
preparation_modifiers.simmering_time: Extended simmering increases histamine from fish products

foods.notes: Extremely high histamine from fermented fish sauce and shrimp paste. High shellfish and fish allergens. Very high salicylates from lemongrass, galangal, and lime. Fructans from garlic and shallots. Amines from fermented products. Histamine increases dramatically with cooking time. One of the highest-histamine soups in Asian cuisine.

foods.name: Pho Broth (Beef)

preparation_modifiers.simmering_duration: Histamine increases exponentially with cooking time; traditional 8-12+ hours = very high histamine
preparation_modifiers.bone_type: Beef bones contain collagen and amino acids that convert to histamine during long cooking
preparation_modifiers.spices: Star anise, cinnamon, and cloves add moderate salicylates

foods.notes: Histamine dramatically elevated from long bone broth simmering (traditional 8-12+ hours). Histamine formation from amino acid decarboxylation during extended cooking. Bone and beef contain bioactive amines. Spices (star anise, cinnamon, cloves) moderately salicylate. Short-simmered pho (2-4 hours) has significantly lower histamine. One of the primary histamine concerns in Asian cuisine.

foods.name: Spring Roll Wrapper (Rice Paper)

preparation_modifiers.composition: Rice flour and water only; minimal processing
preparation_modifiers.filling_dependent: Wrapper itself very safe; allergen risk comes from fillings

foods.name: Cardamom (Green)
foods.notes: High salicylate spice. Member of ginger family (Zingiberaceae). May cross-react with ginger. Can trigger reactions in salicylate-sensitive individuals. Source: Swain AR et al., salicylate content of foods, JADA 1985; Monash FODMAP app.

foods.name: Garlic Powder
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (fructans) — concentrated form of fresh garlic. Even small amounts can trigger IBS symptoms. Histamine liberator. Source: Monash University Low FODMAP Diet App 2023; Gibson & Shepherd, Gastroenterology 2010.

foods.name: Onion Powder
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (fructans). Concentrated dehydrated onion — 1 tsp equivalent to significant portion of fresh onion. Major IBS trigger. Source: Monash University FODMAP App 2023; Barrett JS et al., J Hum Nutr Diet 2011.

foods.name: Vanilla Extract
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates. Alcohol-based extraction — may cause reactions in alcohol-sensitive or salicylate-sensitive individuals. Some artificial vanilla (vanillin) may contain sulfites. Source: Swain AR salicylate tables; FSANZ allergen guidance.

foods.name: Chili Powder (Blend)
foods.notes: High salicylates from nightshade-based chili peppers. Blend typically contains cumin, garlic powder, oregano. Very high combined salicylate and amine burden. Source: Swain AR et al., JADA 1985; Joneja JMV, Dealing with Food Allergies 2003.

foods.name: Allspice
foods.notes: Very high salicylates — one of the highest-salicylate spices. Name derives from flavor resembling combination of cloves, nutmeg, and cinnamon. Source: Swain AR et al., salicylate content of foods, JADA 1985.

foods.name: Fenugreek Seed
foods.notes: Legume — can cross-react with peanut and chickpea in legume-sensitized individuals. Moderate-high FODMAP (GOS). High oxalates and lectins. Used medicinally; may affect blood sugar. Source: Srivastava AK et al., Indian J Allergy 2010; Monash FODMAP app.

foods.name: Star Anise
foods.notes: High salicylates. Anethole is the primary compound — cross-reactivity documented with anise seed, fennel, and dill (apiaceae/umbelliferae family). Source: Swain AR JADA 1985; Niggemann B, Wahn U, Allergy 1999.

foods.name: Sumac
foods.notes: Very high salicylates. Anacardiaceae family — cross-reactivity potential with cashew, mango, and poison ivy. High tannin content. Common in Middle Eastern cuisine. Source: Swain AR 1985; Caballero T et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2003.

foods.name: Mustard Seed (Yellow)
foods.notes: Mustard is a top-14 EU allergen and major Canadian allergen. Cross-reactivity with other Brassica species (cabbage, broccoli, radish). High nickel. Source: EFSA mustard allergen review 2018; Morisset M et al., Allergy 2003.

foods.name: Grapeseed Oil
foods.notes: Mild salicylate content. Derived from wine-making byproduct — may contain trace sulfites from grape processing. Generally well-tolerated. High smoke point. Source: Chung SY et al., J Agric Food Chem 2007.

foods.name: Palm Oil
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Nearly allergen-free. Saturated fat content limits its use in heart-healthy protocols. Environmental controversy but clinically very low reactivity. Source: FSANZ food allergy database; FAO lipid composition tables.

foods.name: Corn Oil
foods.notes: Trace gluten in some brands due to shared processing with wheat. Refined corn oil is generally hypoallergenic. Corn protein allergens are substantially removed in refined oil. Source: Taylor SL et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 1997; FARE corn allergy guidance.

foods.name: Duck Fat
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Monounsaturated fat profile similar to olive oil. Low-moderate histamine from poultry fat — increases with storage/heat. Prized in French cuisine. Source: USDA FoodData Central; Maintz L & Novak N, Am J Clin Nutr 2007.

foods.name: MCT Oil
foods.notes: Essentially allergen-free. Derived from coconut or palm kernel oil. GI intolerance (cramping, diarrhea) can occur when introduced rapidly — not an allergy response. No known cross-reactivity. Source: Rego Costa AC et al., Nutr Hosp 2012; Vandenberghe C et al., Nutrition 2020.

foods.name: Hemp Seed Oil
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Cold-pressed hemp seed oil. Not the same as CBD oil. Contains optimal omega-3:omega-6 ratio. No psychoactive compounds. Source: Callaway J, Euphytica 2004; USDA FoodData Central.

foods.name: Pumpkin Seed Oil
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Dark green specialty oil, not suitable for high-heat cooking. May cross-react with other cucurbits (squash, melon) in rare cases. Source: Procida G et al., J Sci Food Agric 2013.

foods.name: Tallow (Beef Fat)
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Beef fat protein content is essentially zero after rendering. Alpha-gal syndrome patients should use caution — mammalian-derived fats may contain galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose. Source: USDA FoodData Central; Steinke JW et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2015.

foods.name: Almond Oil
foods.notes: HIGH TREE NUT ALLERGEN — derived from almonds. Although allergen protein content is reduced in refined oil, cold-pressed/unrefined almond oil retains significant protein. Contraindicated for tree nut-allergic individuals unless confirmed refined. Cross-reactive with peach, cherry, apricot (Rosaceae). Source: Taylor SL et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 1997; Teuber SS et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 1997.

foods.name: Vegetable Shortening
foods.notes: Moderate soy content — most shortenings use partially hydrogenated soybean or palm oil. May contain soy protein traces. Trans fat content variable (modern formulations reduce this). Source: FDA trans fat guidance; USDA FoodData Central.

foods.name: Burger Patty (Generic)
foods.notes: Amines increase significantly with cooking (higher heat = more biogenic amines). Soy added as filler in many commercial patties. Well-done patties accumulate heterocyclic amines. Alpha-gal syndrome risk for tick-bite sensitized individuals. Source: Sinha R et al., JNCI 1994; Commins SP et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2009.

foods.name: Fried Chicken (Generic)
foods.notes: Very high gluten from wheat breading. High composite allergen burden — contains gluten, egg (in batter), soy (common in frying oils). Sodium content high. Source: McDonald's allergen info; FARE allergen guidance for fried foods.

foods.name: Ranch Dressing
foods.notes: High dairy (buttermilk base) and egg (mayonnaise base). Significant histamine from buttermilk fermentation. Many bottled versions contain MSG and preservatives. Source: Hidden Valley Ranch ingredient list; Joneja JMV histamine food tables.

foods.name: BBQ Sauce
foods.notes: High histamine (tomato base + vinegar + smoke = major histamine liberators). Very high fructose (HFCS in most commercial sauces). High salicylates from tomato, vinegar, spices. Sulfites added as preservative. Source: Maintz L & Novak N, AJCN 2007; USDA food database.

foods.name: Breakfast Burrito (Generic)
foods.notes: Very high composite allergen load — wheat (tortilla), egg, dairy (cheese), and soy (sausage fillers) all present. Significant FODMAP burden from flour tortilla + onion/garlic seasoning. Source: McDonald's Breakfast Burrito allergen data; Taco Bell allergen guide.

foods.name: Nachos (Restaurant Style)
foods.notes: Significant dairy burden from processed cheese sauce. Corn chips are lower gluten but often contaminated. Jalapeños and salsa toppings raise salicylate and histamine burden substantially. Source: Applebee's/restaurant chain allergen menus; Swain AR 1985.

foods.name: Fish Sandwich (Generic Fast Food)
foods.notes: Very high fish allergen (cod or pollock in most fast-food versions). Tartar sauce contains egg. Shared fryers risk shellfish cross-contamination. Bun contains gluten and soy. Source: McDonald's Filet-O-Fish allergen sheet; FARE fish allergy guidance.

foods.name: Chicken Quesadilla (Restaurant)
foods.notes: Very high gluten (flour tortilla) and dairy (melted cheese). Significant lactose burden. FODMAP fructan load from flour tortilla. Source: Taco Bell allergen menu; Chipotle allergen info 2024.

foods.name: Caesar Salad (Restaurant)
foods.notes: High composite allergen burden. Classic Caesar dressing contains anchovy (fish), egg (raw/coddled), parmesan (dairy). Croutons add gluten. Significant histamine from anchovy + parmesan. Source: Bon Appetit classic caesar recipe; FARE fish allergy info.

foods.name: Onion Rings (Generic)
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (fructans) from onions — major IBS trigger. High gluten from batter. Onion content makes this a significant fructan source even in small servings. Source: Monash FODMAP app; Burger King onion ring allergen data.

foods.name: Coffee Creamer (Powdered)
foods.notes: Typically soy-based with high corn syrup solids (fructose). Despite 'non-dairy' label, many contain casein (milk protein). Check labels carefully. Sodium caseinate is a milk derivative — not suitable for dairy-allergic. Source: FDA labeling rules; Coffee-mate ingredient list.

foods.name: Non-Dairy Creamer (Liquid)
foods.notes: Contains sodium caseinate (dairy protein) despite 'non-dairy' name. High fructose from sugar and corn syrup. Artificial flavors may cause reactions in sensitive individuals. Source: FDA dairy labeling; International Delight ingredient list 2024.

foods.name: Whipped Topping (Non-Dairy)
foods.notes: Contains sodium caseinate (milk derivative) and soy. Despite 'non-dairy' marketing, it is NOT safe for dairy-allergic individuals. High in partially hydrogenated oils in older formulations; newer versions use palm oil. Source: FDA; Cool Whip ingredient list.

foods.name: Canned Chickpeas (Packaged)
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (GOS + fructans) — major IBS trigger. High nickel. Rinsing canned chickpeas reduces FODMAP content by ~25-35%. Aquafaba (liquid) is very high in oligosaccharides. Cross-reactive with other legumes. Source: Monash University FODMAP app; Bohn L et al., J Agric Food Chem 2008.

foods.name: Rice Cakes (Plain)
foods.notes: Low allergen burden. Trace gluten from shared manufacturing. High glycemic index. Flavored varieties add significant allergen risk (cheese, caramel = dairy; peanut butter = peanuts). Source: USDA FoodData Central; Quaker allergen statement.

foods.name: English Muffin
foods.notes: Very high gluten — wheat-based yeast bread. Very high FODMAP (fructans). Contains dairy and egg in most commercial recipes. Nooks and crannies create higher surface area for toasting-related Maillard reaction compounds. Source: Thomas' English Muffin allergen data; Monash FODMAP.

foods.name: Bagel (Plain)
foods.notes: Very high gluten (high-gluten bread flour) and very high FODMAP (fructans). Lower egg and dairy than other breads but still present in commercial varieties. Sesame seed bagels are a top sesame allergen risk. Source: Monash University FODMAP; FARE wheat allergy guidance.

foods.name: Frozen Waffles
foods.notes: High gluten, dairy, and egg — multi-allergen food. Buttermilk varieties increase lactose and dairy content. Commonly eaten by children — important for early allergen screening. Source: Kellogg's Eggo allergen statement; FARE multi-allergen foods.

foods.name: Microwave Popcorn
foods.notes: Butter-flavored varieties contain dairy. Shared manufacturing may introduce gluten. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) concern in older microwave bag coatings — now largely phased out. Source: USDA FoodData Central; FSANZ food allergy data.

foods.name: Granola (Plain)
foods.notes: Variable gluten — oats carry cross-contamination risk with wheat. Tree nut content depends on recipe. High fructose from honey/dried fruit. Nickel moderately high from oats. Most commercial granola contains added oil and sweeteners. Source: Monash FODMAP; Celiac Disease Foundation oat guidance.

foods.name: Canned Lentils
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (GOS + fructans). High nickel — relevant for nickel-contact dermatitis. Rinsing reduces oligosaccharides ~25-30%. Cross-reactive with other legumes in sensitized individuals. Source: Monash FODMAP app 2023; Bohn L et al., J Agric Food Chem 2008.

foods.name: Corn Flakes
foods.notes: Contains malt flavoring (barley malt extract) — significant gluten despite being corn-based. NOT safe for celiac disease or gluten intolerance. High GI. Fortified with iron. Source: Kellogg's allergen statement; Celiac Disease Foundation malt guidance.

foods.name: Coconut Water
foods.notes: FDA classifies coconut as a tree nut, though it is botanically a fruit. Coconut allergy is distinct from tree nut allergy and relatively rare. High natural sugars and polyols — caution with FODMAP/fructose malabsorption. Source: FDA tree nut classification; Monash FODMAP app.

foods.name: Rice Milk
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden — suitable for dairy, soy, tree nut, and egg-free diets. Made from milled rice and water. Trace gluten risk if rice is processed with wheat equipment. Higher glycemic index than other plant milks. Source: USDA FoodData Central; Allergen Bureau rice milk assessment.

foods.name: Hard Cider (Alcoholic)
foods.notes: High histamine from fermentation. Very high fructose — caution with fructose malabsorption. Significant sulfites (preservative and natural from fermentation). High salicylates from apple skin. Dry ciders have less residual sugar but more histamine. Source: Maintz L & Novak N 2007; Monash FODMAP.

foods.name: Matcha Latte
foods.notes: Very high oxalates — matcha is a concentrated powdered green tea and one of the highest oxalate foods/beverages. High salicylates. Milk content varies by preparation. Caffeine content moderate-high. Source: Massey LK et al., oxalate content of foods, JADA 2001; Higdon JV & Frei B, Crit Rev Food Sci 2006.

foods.name: Oolong Tea
foods.notes: Moderate-high salicylates and oxalates. Falls between green tea (lower oxidation) and black tea (fully oxidized) in histamine/amine content. Moderate caffeine. Tannins bind to minerals — may reduce iron absorption. Source: Beecher GR, J Nutr 2003; Noonan SC & Savage GP, Asia Pac J Clin Nutr 1999.

foods.name: Hibiscus Tea (Agua de Jamaica)
foods.notes: High salicylates and moderate-high oxalates. Notable anthocyanin content. Hibiscus can interact with antihypertensive medications (additive effect). Histamine liberator. Used widely in Latin American and African cuisines. Source: Hopkins AL et al., J Ethnopharmacol 2013; Swain AR salicylate tables 1985.

foods.name: Chai Tea Latte
foods.notes: Spice blend (cardamom, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, black pepper) adds significant salicylates and moderate oxalates. Dairy base adds lactose. Common additions like vanilla syrup add fructose. Source: Swain AR 1985; Starbucks allergen guide 2024.

foods.name: Ginger Tea (Brewed)
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates. Anti-nausea and anti-inflammatory properties well-documented. Ginger family (Zingiberaceae) may cross-react with cardamom. Generally anti-histamine in small amounts but can be pro-histamine in large doses. Source: Zingiberaceae cross-reactivity literature; Swain AR 1985.

foods.name: Turmeric Latte (Golden Milk)
foods.notes: High salicylates from turmeric. Often combined with black pepper (piperine) to enhance curcumin bioavailability. Turmeric can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals. Moderate histamine. Source: Swain AR 1985; Anand P et al., Mol Pharm 2007.

foods.name: Lemon Water (Infused)
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates from citrus. Histamine liberator — lemon is a non-histamine food but liberates histamine in cells. OAS (oral allergy syndrome) reported in birch pollen-sensitized individuals. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; Ballmer-Weber BK et al., Allergy 2002.

foods.name: Papaya
foods.notes: High histamine liberator. Contains papain (proteolytic enzyme) — major latex cross-reactive food. Latex-fruit syndrome risk: patients with latex allergy may react. Ripe papaya has more amines and histamine than unripe. Source: Brehler R et al., Allergy 1997; Reider N et al., Contact Dermatitis 2001.

foods.name: Grapefruit
foods.notes: High salicylates and histamine. Contains furanocoumarins (naringenin) that inhibit CYP3A4 — major drug-grapefruit interaction (statins, calcium channel blockers, immunosuppressants). Not a clinical food allergy risk for most but pharmacologically significant. Source: Bailey DG et al., CMAJ 1998; Swain AR 1985.

foods.name: Plum
foods.notes: High salicylates. High sorbitol (polyols) — significant IBS trigger. Birch pollen OAS (oral allergy syndrome) commonly causes tingling/itching with fresh plum in pollen-allergic individuals. Prunes (dried plums) have much higher FODMAP and salicylate content. Source: Swain AR 1985; Monash FODMAP; Ballmer-Weber 2002.

foods.name: Raspberry
foods.notes: Very high salicylates — among the highest of all berries. Moderate-high oxalates. Birch pollen OAS risk. Histamine liberator. Seeds contain significant amounts of raspberry seed oil (vitamin E). Source: Swain AR 1985; Noonan SC & Savage GP, Asia Pac J Clin Nutr 1999.

foods.name: Cantaloupe
foods.notes: Moderate histamine. Latex-fruit syndrome and ragweed pollen OAS cross-reactivity (cantaloupe and ragweed share proteins). Most well-tolerated melon. High vitamin A precursor. Source: Brehler R et al., Allergy 1997; Ballmer-Weber BK, Allergy 2002.

foods.name: Pomegranate
foods.notes: High salicylates. High fructose — caution with fructose malabsorption. Rich in polyphenols (punicalagins). Some reports of allergic reactions (mostly contact) in latex-sensitive patients. Juice has higher salicylate/histamine concentration than whole fruit. Source: Swain AR 1985; Seeram NP, J Agric Food Chem 2008.

foods.name: Blackberry
foods.notes: Very high salicylates and high oxalates. Major histamine liberator. One of the highest-salicylate fruits. Birch pollen OAS. Significant tannin content (astringent). Source: Swain AR 1985; Noonan SC & Savage GP 1999.

foods.name: Apricot
foods.notes: High sorbitol (polyols) — major IBS trigger. High salicylates. Dried apricots: dramatically more concentrated fructose, polyols, and salicylates, and typically preserved with sulfites. Birch/tree pollen OAS very common. Source: Swain AR 1985; Monash FODMAP; Ballmer-Weber 2002.

foods.name: Fig (Fresh)
foods.notes: High histamine liberator, very high fructose. Latex cross-reactivity (contains ficin, a latex-related protease). One of the highest fructose fruits. Dried figs are even more concentrated. OAS with birch pollen reported. Source: Brehler R et al., Allergy 1997; Monash FODMAP app.

foods.name: Honeydew Melon
foods.notes: Low-moderate allergen burden. Better tolerated than cantaloupe in most melon-sensitive individuals. Latex-fruit and ragweed pollen OAS risk. High water content. Source: Ballmer-Weber BK, Allergy 2002; Brehler R 1997.

foods.name: Globe Artichoke
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (fructans) — one of the highest fructan-containing vegetables. Asteraceae (daisy) family — cross-reactivity with mugwort pollen and other Asteraceae (chicory, dandelion). Canned artichoke has significantly higher histamine. Source: Monash University FODMAP; Hemmer W et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 1997.

foods.name: Leek
foods.notes: High FODMAP (fructans) particularly in the white/light green portion. Green leek tops are lower FODMAP and better tolerated. Allium family — same cross-reactivity as onion and garlic. Source: Monash University FODMAP 2023; Barrett JS & Gibson PR, J Hum Nutr Diet 2012.

foods.name: Radish
foods.notes: Moderate salicylates. Brassicaceae family — cross-reactivity with cabbage, broccoli, mustard. Pickled daikon (tsukemono) has high histamine from fermentation. Goitrogenic compounds — relevant for thyroid patients. Source: Swain AR 1985; Brassica cross-reactivity literature.

foods.name: Brussels Sprouts
foods.notes: Moderate FODMAP (fructans) and moderate-high oxalates. High nickel content. Cooking reduces lectin content. Brassica family — cross-reactivity with cabbage, mustard, radish. Sulfur-containing compounds may worsen bloating in IBS. Source: Monash FODMAP; Swain AR 1985; Noonan & Savage 1999.

foods.name: Cucumber
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden when fresh. Pickles have dramatically higher histamine from fermentation/pickling. Ragweed pollen OAS — raw cucumber may cause oral allergy symptoms. Cucurbit family cross-reactivity (melon, squash, zucchini). Source: Ballmer-Weber BK 2002; Monash FODMAP.

foods.name: Venison (Fresh)
foods.notes: Low allergen burden — lean game meat. Alpha-gal syndrome risk (tick-bite sensitization to mammalian meat). Histamine increases with aging/storage. Wild vs. farmed venison may have different exposure risks. Source: Commins SP et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2009; USDA FoodData Central.

foods.name: Bison (Ground)
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Leanest of the mammalian meats — lower fat means slightly lower amine accumulation. Alpha-gal syndrome risk. May cross-react with beef in beef-allergic individuals. Source: Commins SP 2009; USDA FoodData Central bison data.

foods.name: Chicken Thigh (Skin-on)
foods.notes: Dark meat and skin contain more fat and more biogenic amines than breast meat. Slow cooking (braising, crockpot) dramatically increases histamine — a key dietary trigger for histamine intolerance patients. Source: Maintz L & Novak N, AJCN 2007; Jarisch R, Histamine Intolerance 2004.

foods.name: Bone Broth (Beef)
foods.notes: VERY HIGH HISTAMINE — one of the highest histamine foods. Histamine and biogenic amine levels increase dramatically with cooking time. 24-hour slow-cooked broth can exceed histamine thresholds for severely histamine-intolerant patients. Despite health claims, contraindicated for histamine intolerance. Source: Maintz L & Novak N 2007; Jarisch R, Histamine Intolerance 2004.

foods.name: Casein Protein Powder
foods.notes: Very high dairy — derived from cow's milk casein protein. Contraindicated for dairy allergy (milk protein allergy). Moderate lactose. Slow-digesting protein — blood amino acid release over 5-7 hours. Cross-reactive with whey protein in milk-allergic individuals. Source: EFSA dairy allergen report; FARE milk allergy guidance.

foods.name: Oat Bran
foods.notes: Moderate-high nickel content — oats are moderate nickel foods. Gluten risk from shared processing with wheat — seek certified gluten-free oat bran for celiac. Beta-glucan fiber in high amounts may cause bloating. Source: Celiac Disease Foundation oat guidance; Monash FODMAP oat bran.

foods.name: Flaxseed Meal (Ground)
foods.notes: Moderate-high oxalates. High lignan content (phytoestrogens). Ground form has better omega-3 bioavailability than whole seeds. Mucilaginous — bulk-forming laxative effect. Minimal allergenicity but oxalate burden significant for kidney stone-prone patients. Source: Noonan SC & Savage GP 1999; Thompson LU et al., Nutr Cancer 2005.

foods.name: Cacao Nibs (Raw)
foods.notes: Very high nickel, histamine, salicylates, oxalates, and amines. Raw/minimally processed cacao has higher reactivity than processed chocolate. Phenylethylamine (PEA) — a biogenic amine known migraine trigger. Theobromine and caffeine add stimulant effects. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; Swain AR 1985; Noonan & Savage 1999.

foods.name: Acai Powder
foods.notes: High salicylates. Concentrated form — higher reactivity than fresh acai. Rich in anthocyanins and resveratrol. Cross-reactivity with latex-fruit syndrome reported in case studies. High antioxidant ORAC score. Source: Swain AR 1985; Schauss AG et al., J Agric Food Chem 2006.

foods.name: Almond Flour
foods.notes: VERY HIGH TREE NUT ALLERGEN — made from whole blanched almonds. Not safe for tree nut allergic individuals. High oxalates. FODMAP moderate at serving sizes used in baking. Popular gluten-free flour but high in calories and fat. Cross-reactive with peach, cherry (Rosaceae). Source: FARE tree nut allergy guidance; Monash FODMAP almond flour.

foods.name: Coconut Flour
foods.notes: Coconut classified as tree nut by FDA — caution in tree nut-allergic individuals (though true coconut allergy is rare and distinct from tree nut allergy). Very high fiber content — can cause significant GI distress if used in large amounts. Low FODMAP at typical serving sizes. Source: FDA tree nut classification; Monash FODMAP coconut flour.

foods.name: Wild Rice
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Technically a grass seed, not true rice. Gluten-free. Higher protein content than white rice. Low FODMAP. Cooked wild rice has distinctive chewy texture and earthy flavor. Source: USDA FoodData Central; Monash FODMAP wild rice.

foods.name: Sorghum
foods.notes: Gluten-free ancient grain. Moderate lectins — cooking and popping reduce lectin content. Major world grain crop. Used in gluten-free brewing. Low FODMAP. Sorghum protein is less digestible than wheat. Source: USDA; Celiac Disease Foundation; Monash FODMAP.

foods.name: Couscous
foods.notes: Very high gluten (durum wheat semolina). Very high FODMAP (fructans). Despite looking like a grain, it is actually a pasta (processed semolina). NOT suitable for celiac or FODMAP-restricted diets. Source: Monash University FODMAP 2023; FARE wheat allergy.

foods.name: Cassava (Tapioca)
foods.notes: Very low allergen burden. Naturally gluten-free starch. Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) — must be properly cooked. Processed tapioca starch is safe. Common in gluten-free baking and bubble tea pearls. Source: FAO cassava processing guidelines; USDA FoodData Central.

foods.name: Injera (Ethiopian Flatbread)
foods.notes: Fermented teff-based flatbread — fermentation significantly increases histamine and biogenic amines. Teff is gluten-free but high in nickel. Naturally sour due to 2-3 day fermentation. Served with stews. Source: USDA FoodData Central; Maintz & Novak 2007.

foods.name: Gazpacho
foods.notes: Very high histamine — raw tomatoes + vinegar + raw cucumber/pepper = major histamine and liberator load. Very high salicylates. Raw preparation concentrates all reactive compounds without cooking reduction. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; Swain AR 1985.

foods.name: Gyro Meat (Lamb/Beef)
foods.notes: High histamine and amines from processed/spiced meat loaf. Sulfites used as preservatives. Gluten from fillers (bread crumbs). Typically served in pita (adds gluten burden). Alpha-gal risk. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; EU food additive database for sulfite use.

foods.name: Bibimbap Rice Bowl
foods.notes: Complex composite dish — multiple allergen exposure. Gochujang (chili paste) is a fermented condiment significantly increasing histamine and salicylates. Sesame oil is a common topping. High nickel from vegetables and sesame. Source: Korean Ministry of Food; Maintz & Novak 2007.

foods.name: Borscht (Beet Soup)
foods.notes: High oxalates from beets (beta vulgaris — high oxalate vegetable). Sour cream topping adds dairy/lactose. Moderate histamine. Beets are high FODMAP (polyols + fructose). Rich in folate and betalains. Source: Noonan & Savage 1999; Monash FODMAP beets.

foods.name: Pesto Sauce (Basil)
foods.notes: High tree nut (pine nuts) and dairy (parmesan). Basil and pine nuts both have moderate salicylates. Parmesan is aged — histamine content higher than fresh dairy. Increasingly common substitutes: walnuts, almonds, or nutritional yeast. Source: FARE tree nut guidance; Swain AR 1985.

foods.name: Miso Ramen (Bowl)
foods.notes: Very high histamine and amines — miso (fermented), fish cake, dried fish toppings (nori), cured pork all contribute. Very high gluten (ramen noodles). Major soy allergen (miso). Significant shellfish cross-contamination risk. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; Japanese Ministry of Health allergen food list.

foods.name: Jerk Chicken
foods.notes: Very high salicylates from jerk spice blend (allspice, scotch bonnet peppers, thyme, cinnamon, black pepper). Nightshade-based hot peppers. Histamine from prolonged marination. High composite spice burden. Source: Swain AR 1985; traditional jerk spice composition.

foods.name: Dahl Makhani (Lentil & Kidney Bean)
foods.notes: Very high FODMAP (GOS + fructans) from black lentils and kidney beans. High nickel. Butter and cream add dairy. Pressure cooking significantly reduces lectins and some oligosaccharides. High protein but major IBS trigger. Source: Monash FODMAP; Bohn L et al. 2008.

foods.name: Jackfruit (Canned, Unripe)
foods.notes: Latex cross-reactivity (Moraceae family with figs, mulberry). Unripe canned jackfruit used as meat substitute — low in fructose. Ripe jackfruit is sweet and very high in fructose. Canning liquid may add sulfites. Source: Brehler R 1997; Moraceae latex cross-reactivity literature.

foods.name: Green Smoothie (Spinach/Kale Base)
foods.notes: Very high oxalates — spinach is one of the highest oxalate foods. High nickel from leafy greens. Concentrated form means higher reactivity than eating leaves whole. Significant risk for kidney stone formation in oxalate-sensitive individuals. Source: Noonan & Savage 1999; Massey LK et al. 2001.

foods.name: Kale
foods.notes: High oxalates — concentrated leafy green. Raw kale can inhibit thyroid (goitrogenic) in very large amounts. Cooking reduces oxalates by ~30-40% and lectins. Brassica family cross-reactivity. High vitamin K — warfarin interaction. Source: Noonan & Savage 1999; USDA FoodData Central.

foods.name: Cream of Wheat (Farina)
foods.notes: Very high gluten (finely milled wheat/semolina). Very high FODMAP (fructans). NOT suitable for celiac or gluten-sensitive individuals. Often prepared with milk, adding dairy burden. High glycemic index. Source: FARE wheat allergy guidance; Monash FODMAP wheat.

foods.name: Nutritional Yeast Flakes
foods.notes: Moderate histamine and amines — deactivated but fermented yeast retains histamine/amine content. Mold-sensitive individuals and those with yeast-reactive conditions may react. High in B12 (fortified versions). Naturally occurring glutamates contribute to umami flavor. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; Joneja JMV, Dealing with Food Allergies 2003.

foods.name: Canned Tuna (Oil-Packed)
foods.notes: VERY HIGH HISTAMINE — oil-packed canned tuna has higher histamine than water-packed due to oil preserving histamine released during canning. Biogenic amines (histamine, scombrotoxin) accumulate during storage. Significant fish allergen. Soy from oil or added fillers. Source: Maintz & Novak 2007; FDA histamine/scombroid fish guidance.

foods.name: Soy Sauce Packet (Takeout)
